study.title: Enhancing title and abstract screening for systematic reviews with GPT-3.5 turbo
study.task_note: Single-case research letter comparing eight prompts given to GPT-3.5 Turbo against three human screeners on the 330 records retrieved by replicating the search of one published systematic review, 'Light Therapy in Insomnia Disorder', with that review's inclusion list as the gold standard.

E01.quote: These numpy arrays, along with the numpy arrays generated by the researchers, were employed to compute sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and the F1 score for both the researchers and the prompts
E01.note: Values for all four metrics for eight prompts and three human screeners are tabulated in online supplementary table 2, fetched at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10850650/supplementaryFiles (file bmjebm-2023-112678supp002.pdf).

E02.quote: a recently published SR titled ‘Light Therapy in Insomnia Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis’ was selected, and the databases were queried using the keywords stipulated in the original paper
E02.note: The source review is named and the record count is given elsewhere in the same paragraph as 330 citations, but the number of records included by the human reference standard is never reported in the letter, in either supplementary table, or in the repository.

E03.searched: Searched the full letter, both BMJ supplementary tables (prompt texts and performance metrics) and the repository output files for a count or proportion of included records; only the total of 330 citations is reported, so inclusion prevalence cannot be taken from reported counts without back-calculating from rounded sensitivity values.

E04.searched: Searched for screening time, hours saved, workload or workload reduction, number of records a human would not need to see, monetary cost, token counts and recall after a human verification step; the letter reports only per-record model and human metrics.

E05.quote: However, it is imperative to recognise that GPT is not yet fully capable of independently completing this task and should be employed as an assistant to mitigate the risk of overlooking potential studies
E05.note: The intended role is stated as an assistant rather than a sole screener, and the following sentences keep humans in the loop by advising researchers to manually screen a proportion of titles and abstracts. The division of labour is not specified any more precisely than that.

E06.searched: Searched for adjudication, consensus, third reviewer, conflict, override, escalation and any rule for resolving model versus human disagreement; the only related sentence recommends combining the findings of different prompts, which the authors state was unexplored in the study.

E07.location: Main text, rationale for choosing the source review
E07.quote: reviewers did not face much trouble but models had difficulties with studies that included patients with secondary sleeping troubles like patients with cancer
E07.note: A population that the model handled badly is named, namely patients with secondary sleep problems such as cancer patients, but the letter does not frame this as a differential exclusion or equity risk, states no equity goal, and reports no disaggregated error rates for that group.

E08a.searched: Searched the methods for any planned stratification or subgroup comparison by topic, study design, population, language, setting or record source; the design compares prompts and human screeners over one undivided record set.

E08b.searched: Searched the results paragraph and supplementary table 2 for performance broken down by any record-level subgroup; the table reports only overall sensitivity, specificity, F1 and accuracy per prompt and per screener.

E08c.searched: Searched for language, non-English, translation, country, region and setting comparisons; the eligibility criteria restrict the corpus to English publications and no performance figures are reported by language or region.

E09.searched: Searched for a target or minimum sensitivity, an acceptable miss rate, a tolerance threshold, and any attribution of such a threshold to Cochrane, PRISMA or another norm; the letter sets no performance target and names no standard setter.

E10.searched: Searched for survey, interview, questionnaire, usability, satisfaction, perceived workload and any elicited reviewer opinion; the three screeners contributed screening decisions as a comparator only and two of them were kept blind to the study objective.

E11.quote: should be employed as an assistant to mitigate the risk of overlooking potential studies
E11.note: Missing eligible studies is named as the critical failure mode, and the reported sensitivities fall as low as 0.38 for two prompts in supplementary table 2. Hallucinated eligibility reasoning and run to run inconsistency are not named.

E12.quote: We advise researchers wanting to deploy GPT to manually screen a proportion of titles and abstracts, experiment with different prompts and consider the combination of findings, a method unexplored in our study
E12.note: A mitigation against relying on the model alone is recommended, namely manual screening of a proportion of records plus assistant only use, but over-reliance, automation bias and alert fatigue are never named and no interaction failure was tested.

E13.quote: GPT is a potent tool, and we propose its usage in title and abstract screening for SRs, following the method we have delineated in this case report, alongside other researchers
E13.note: Intended use is title and abstract screening alongside researchers; the scope limit is set in the next paragraphs, which rule out independent completion of the task and state that the single-case findings are not generalisable and that each study objective needs its own prompt format.

E14.quote: The code for this process is available at the provided link: https://github.com/mamishere/Article-Relevancy-Extraction-GPT3.5-Turbo
E14.note: Repository fetched and resolves. It contains Relevancy Extraction Notebook.ipynb with all eight prompts and the API call, data/data.txt with the 330 records, and output files. Only a bare URL is given, with no commit, tag or archive DOI; the head commit at the time of extraction was 19c72abdbaee25e07284e8ff9c949f9de0169e9f dated 2024-08-18. Prompt texts are additionally in supplementary table 1.

E15.quote: GPT-4 has exhibited commendable performance across a range of human-related tasks and has surpassed its predecessor, GPT-3.5, in evaluations conducted by the company
E15.note: Prior evidence about GPT model performance is cited, but no rationale is given for evaluating GPT-3.5 rather than the GPT-4 model the same sentence describes as superior. The two stated selection rationales in the letter concern the choice of source review, not the choice of model.

E16.quote: The labels used as the ‘gold standard’ were the studies included in the selected SR
E16.note: The reference standard is final inclusion in the named published review. The screening procedure used by that review's authors is not described here, so provenance is stated at the level of the source review only.

E17.location: Repository: https://github.com/mamishere/Article-Relevancy-Extraction-GPT3.5-Turbo, file 'Relevancy Extraction Notebook.ipynb', function generate_prompt
E17.quote:
model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": prompt}],
        max_tokens=100,         # Set a limit on the response length
        temperature=0,          # Set the temperature for randomness (0 means deterministic)
E17.note: Fetched at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mamishere/Article-Relevancy-Extraction-GPT3.5-Turbo/main/Relevancy%20Extraction%20Notebook.ipynb . Temperature 0, max_tokens 100, n=1, no stop sequence and no structured output constraint. None of these parameters appear in the published letter or in either supplementary table.

E18.quote: The prompt texts are available in the online supplemental table 1
E18.note: Supplement fetched at https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10850650/supplementaryFiles ; file bmjebm-2023-112678supp001.pdf is titled 'Supplementary table 1. Prompts text' and reproduces all eight prompts in full. The same eight prompts appear as f-strings in the repository notebook.

E19.quote: Lastly, Prompt 8 introduced a screening tool with four questions, requiring the model to include a study if the answer to all four questions was ‘Yes’ or ‘Unsure
E19.note: Prompt 8 carries an explicit Unsure option that routes the record onward to full-text screening, and prompts 4, 5, 6 and 7 instruct the model to include studies it is uncertain about. The prompts contain no instruction to defer to a named human reviewer.

E20.quote: Prompt 1, which replicated the criteria from the original paper, demonstrated 80% accuracy and 62% sensitivity
E20.note: The criteria supplied to the model are the source review's own criteria, reproduced as criteria A to D in supplementary table 1 and in the repository notebook. Later prompts deliberately loosen those criteria, and the letter says so.

E21.quote: We also recommend the incorporation of a sentence prioritising inclusivity to guide the model in including unclear studies
E21.note: The inclusivity sentence is an explicit recall over precision configuration; the letter reports that it raised sensitivity and lowered specificity.

E22.searched: Searched for training data, knowledge cutoff, September 2021, contamination, leakage and memorisation; the source review was published in 2023 and the letter never considers whether the model had seen it.

E23.searched: Searched for hallucination, fabricated or specious reasoning, prompt injection, jailbreak, adversarial input and misuse; none is documented and none is tested. The model was constrained to a binary 0 or 1 output and only aggregate agreement with the gold standard was measured.

E24.quote: Prompt 7 assessed the impact of phrasing by modifying the language of the previous prompt and providing a more detailed description of the inclusivity phrase
E24.note: Eight prompt variants were run over the same records and wording sensitivity was tested directly. Repeat-run consistency was not tested; each prompt was run once at temperature 0.

E25.quote: The initial search yielded 330 citations, which were subsequently imported into EndNote X20. An RTF file containing titles and abstracts was generated, followed by its conversion into a more compatible TXT format, thus facilitating further data processing
E25.note: The collection method is described and the record set itself is published in the repository as data/data.txt, and limitations of the corpus are discussed, but the databases searched are never named and there is no dedicated dataset documentation.

E26.note: A system card equivalent is cited, but it documents GPT-4, not the evaluated model GPT-3.5 Turbo, and it is cited for performance claims rather than for transparency. No documentation for GPT-3.5 Turbo is cited and transparency is not considered in model choice.

E27.quote: The integration of the OpenAI GPT 3.5 Turbo API played a pivotal role in advancing our research
E27.note: The model family is named but no dated snapshot is pinned. The repository shows model="gpt-3.5-turbo", which is a rolling alias rather than a pinned version such as gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, and neither the letter nor the repository reports an access or run date.

E28.quote: The initial search yielded 330 citations, which were subsequently imported into EndNote X20
E28.note: All 330 records from the replicated search were screened, with no balancing or sampling, through the production OpenAI API. The records are a replication of the source review's search rather than that review's own record set.

E29.quote: the lack of clarity in the criteria for ‘sleep troubles’ resulted in substantial bias in the model’s performance and significant disparities among researchers
E29.note: Error sources are discussed qualitatively, namely an ambiguous population definition and difficulty with secondary sleep problems, but no misclassified records are examined, counted or categorised, and no false negative is identified.

E30.quote: The integration of the OpenAI GPT 3.5 Turbo API played a pivotal role in advancing our research. This powerful tool enabled us to initiate requests to evaluate the pertinence of prompts to individual papers
E30.note: Access route is the OpenAI API called per record, with results collected in a pandas dataframe, and EndNote X20 is named as the reference manager. The repository notebook additionally shows a 21 second sleep between calls and rotation across seven API keys.

E31.quote: It needs to be acknowledged that the findings of this single-case study are not generalisable, and each study objective necessitates its distinct format
E31.note: The research letter has no limitations section. Generalisability, the ambiguous population criterion and imperfect human performance are acknowledged in running discussion, but uncertainties around the model's failure modes are not documented systematically.

E32.searched: Searched for a list or description of the eligible records the model missed, any false negative case discussion, and any tail or worst-case figure beyond the per-prompt averages in supplementary table 2; the letter names no individual missed study and reports no worst-case analysis.

E33.searched: Searched for a protocol, pre-specification, pre-registration, or any rule stating in advance what performance would justify adoption, limited deployment or rejection; the letter reports metrics and then gives narrative advice.

E34.searched: Searched the text and supplementary table 2 for confidence intervals, 95%, standard deviation, standard error, credible interval or any other uncertainty measure; only point estimates to two decimal places are given.

E35.searched: Searched for energy, carbon, emissions, compute, GPU, tokens consumed and monetary API spend in the letter, both supplements and the repository; none is reported.
